THE UNITED KINGDOM: 4 RULERS SAUL → SOLOMON
Israel's elders asked Samuel for “a king to judge us like all the nations”. The LORD told Samuel that they had rejected him, not Samuel, and to grant it. 1 Samuel 8:4–9 1 Samuel 8:22
Looking for his father's lost asses, Saul came to Samuel, who anointed him privately with a vial of oil “to be captain over his inheritance”. 1 Samuel 9:3–20 1 Samuel 10:1
At Mizpeh the lot fell on Benjamin and then on Saul, who had hidden “among the stuff”. The people shouted, “God save the king”. 1 Samuel 10:17–24
After he rescued Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite, “they made Saul king before the LORD in Gilgal”. 1 Samuel 11:1–15
From the textSo 1 Samuel tells of three steps: a private anointing, a public choice by lot at Mizpeh, and the renewing of the kingdom at Gilgal. 1 Samuel 10:1 1 Samuel 10:24 1 Samuel 11:14–15
ON THE WORLD STAGE: The Philistines · Ammon · Amalek · Moab, Edom and Zobah
“the LORD hath rejected thee from being king over Israel”

Samuel's words after the war with Amalek: Saul “didst evil in the sight of the LORD”, and “Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king”. 1 Samuel 15:19 1 Samuel 15:23
An earlier rebuke came at Gilgal, when Saul offered the burnt offering before Samuel arrived: “now thy kingdom shall not continue”. 1 Samuel 13:8–14
Saul twice answered, “I have sinned”. 1 Samuel 15:24 1 Samuel 15:30

Chronicles adds a reason Samuel's account does not give in its verdict: he asked “counsel of one that had a familiar spirit” and “enquired not of the LORD”. 1 Samuel tells that visit to Endor at length. 1 Chronicles 10:13–14 1 Samuel 28:7–19
David would not harm him, calling him “the LORD's anointed”, and mourned him: “Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives”. 1 Samuel 24:6 1 Samuel 26:9 2 Samuel 1:23
“So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD”

Gibeah and the places of the reign
The united kingdom · tribe of Benjamin. Only places Scripture names are shown, each where the Atlas puts it.
Saul built an altar after Michmash, “the first altar that he built unto the LORD”. 1 Samuel 14:35
He had put “those that had familiar spirits, and the wizards, out of the land”, and then sought one himself. 1 Samuel 28:3 1 Samuel 28:7
He killed the priests of the LORD at Nob. 1 Samuel 22:17–19
He tried to destroy the Gibeonites “in his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah”, though Israel had sworn to spare them. The famine in David's days was laid to this. 2 Samuel 21:1–2
Sa Samuel “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams”
Th The company of prophets Twice Saul prophesied among a company of prophets, near Gibeah and at Naioth in Ramah. The people's saying “Is Saul also among the prophets?” came from this.
Each ribbon joins the two accounts of one matter, passage to passage.
How much of the reign is told

Acts 13:21: forty years. 1 Samuel 13:1 in the KJV reads “Saul reigned one year; and when he had reigned two years over Israel”; the KJV margin gives the Hebrew as “the son of one year in his reigning”. No age at accession survives.
McFall keeps Acts 13:21's forty years and counts back from David's accession in 1010 BC. On p. 477 he writes the span as 1050–1011.
Ussher also takes forty years: Saul made king in the year of the world 2909 (1095 BC); David king in Hebron in 2949 (1055 BC).
No BC years. They hold that numbers have dropped out of 1 Samuel 13:1 and that the reign lasted about twenty or twenty-two years.
The Aramaic Targum, and the Greek version of Symmachus (2nd century AD), as reported by Driver (1890)
The Targum reads “as a child a year old who has no sins, was Saul when he became king”; Symmachus also turns the words into a description rather than an age.[6]
One year after the Philistines were subdued
Ussher read “son of one year” as one year after Samuel subdued the Philistines, and the “two years” as two years Saul reigned free of them, within a reign of forty years.[1]

The verse has the shape of the regular formula, so an age once stood after “son of”. Keil thought Saul was at least forty, since Jonathan already led troops, and that a number such as twenty fell out before “two years”. Driver adds that the whole verse is missing from the Greek Old Testament and may be a late insertion.[5][6]
Wellhausen held that the age was never filled in, and that “two” grew out of the Hebrew word for “year” that follows it.[7]
Dated by an era from David's birth

McFall keeps Acts 13:21's forty years and reads 13:1 as dating Saul's rejection by an era beginning at David's birth, which he puts in 1040 BC. On his reckoning Saul was rejected about 1037 BC, in his fourteenth year.[3]

Saul's age when he became king is not given: the number is missing in 1 Samuel 13:1.
Scripture does not say how many years passed between Saul's anointing and his rejection, or between his rejection and his death.
Scripture does not name Saul's mother.
Scripture does not explain how the woman at Endor brought up Samuel; the text simply calls the figure Samuel (1 Samuel 28:12–16).
Scripture gives no account of Saul's wars with Moab, Edom and the kings of Zobah beyond the list in 1 Samuel 14:47.
1 Samuel 14:49 does not list Ish-bosheth among Saul's sons; it names Jonathan, Ishui and Melchi-shua.
